objects_verbatim.text: WORKER: You came through Rook's hatch? The sentinel takes its shield from the relay upstairs. West stair. I'll keep the others back until you cut it.
objects_verbatim.after: WORKER: Its shield's gone. I'll get everyone who can walk to the stair. Please don't leave the others in the glass.

steps.prompt: The cell speaker crackles. The recovered voices are waiting on the clay plate.

objects_verbatim.locked: The speaker needs the voiceprint from Rook's clay reader. The upstairs relay is still feeding the sentinel's shield.
objects_verbatim.success:
The first worker answers to his name. Others follow, carrying the voice-glass carefully between them. Iona stays until everyone has reached the stair.
Supplies recovered: Ether and Revive.
objects_verbatim.failure: The speaker cuts out under the strain. A voice is caught inside; forcing the case will not release it.
objects_verbatim.done: DARA: I've checked every name. We're all here. Come find us at the Kiln when you've caught your breath.

yes.text:
Life support kept them well.
The medics treat your crew.
Found: a Mid Ether.

no.text:
Reserve air barely lasted.
The medics must stay with
the rescued workers.

objects_verbatim.text: Cleaning drones turn on you.
objects_verbatim.win_text:
The drones scatter.
Found: 40 credits.

objects_verbatim.text:
An emergency locker.
Found: 3 Tonics.

objects_verbatim.locked:
The sentinel stands inside a humming shield.
ROOK: Follow the cable. Its relay is upstairs; we can't reach the glass until that shield is down.

objects_verbatim.text: IONA: Those prisoners are my patients.

scenes.staging_status: noncanonical animation direction; does not add dialogue or alter game events

objects_verbatim.text: The watchbot sounds an alarm.
objects_verbatim.win_text: The watchbot sparks out.

objects_verbatim.text: Sable pulls the shield relay. The cable flashes once, then goes dark. Below, the sentinel turns toward the stair.
objects_verbatim.done: The routing lever is fixed in place. The sentinel's shield has no power.

steps.prompt: The damaged relay can keep one line fully powered. Which do you protect?

objects_verbatim.success: The chosen line holds. The sentinel's shield goes dark.
objects_verbatim.failure: The damaged lever springs back. Neither line has changed.

choice_effects.text: The cells open and the security drones stop. The air pumps switch to their small reserve tanks.
The air pumps keep running. Security drones remain active; the cell speaker will need the recovered voiceprint.

objects_verbatim.text: NELL: I heard him in here. It sounded like he was singing through the wall. Can he still hear me?
objects_verbatim.after: NELL: The lights changed. Did that help him?

variants.text: NELL: The drones stopped. Papa says the air feels thin. Please hurry.
NELL: That's him. That's really him. Papa, I'm here.

objects_verbatim.text:
A guard's kit.
Found: Ether and a Tonic.

scenes.staging_status: noncanonical animation direction; does not add dialogue or alter game events

objects_verbatim.text: MENDER: Rook keeps the insulated tools in the east locker. His reader's on the west bench. Mind the scrubbers—nobody told them the workshop closed.

steps.prompt: A voice catches in the clay reader's groove. What do you do?

objects_verbatim.success: The plate keeps the trapped voices. Beneath them, a familiar phrase begins to answer Sable.
objects_verbatim.failure: The plate is still unread. The trapped voice has not been copied or erased.
objects_verbatim.done: The recovered voiceprint is safe on the plate. It is ready for the cell speaker.

objects_verbatim.text:
The workers' spare arms.
Iron Blade, Iron Bow,
Dart Gun, 2 BronzeHelms.
Equip them from the menu.
Scrubbers rattle in the aisle.
objects_verbatim.win_text:
The workshop falls quiet.
Found: 25 credits.

objects_verbatim.locked:
The cell sentinel holds
Nells father inside the yard.
Free him first. His docket
will open the railway gate.

objects_verbatim.label: Tucked-away bundle
objects_verbatim.text: Behind the old wall trim, a cloth bundle is still dry.

scenes.staging_status: noncanonical animation direction; does not add dialogue or alter game events

steps.prompt: ROOK: The bridge is loose and the kettle's out of tune. Where do we start?

choice_effects.text: You brace the loose bridge. The strings settle into a warm chord. Across the square, Nell waves you toward the lantern.
You retune the kettle until its whistle rests beside the strings. Nell waves from the lantern, impatient for her father's first verse.

objects_verbatim.locked:
Help Rook with the instrument
by the road keeper first.
Then speak to Nell nearby.
objects_verbatim.success: The festival changes.
objects_verbatim.failure: Try again.

Play the recovered voices

The speaker cuts out under the strain. A voice is caught inside; forcing the case will not release it.

The Stolen Song

Nell's father was singing in the square when a furnace bell rang. Now he cannot speak, and his song is playing inside an Orison carriage.
Rook knows a service hatch beneath the loading yard. If we reach the cells before the next train leaves, we can bring him home.

SENTINEL: The worker's voice is registered to Orison.
IONA: His name is on my patient list.
SABLE: And his daughter is waiting outside. Give it back.

For a moment, Nell's father only breathes. Then he says her name.
The workers begin helping one another out of the cells. He presses a creased carriage docket into Sable's hand. This was not the only shipment.

FATHER: Brass drives the dawn train. I heard him arguing with the guards.
SABLE: Where can we find him?
FATHER: The glass viaduct. There's a refuge underneath the west end. Please—my daughter's safe now. Their children are still waiting.
Recover Nell's father's voice without abandoning the people who need the district's heat.
The carriage docket identifies the next shipment: prisoners leaving the glass viaduct at dawn.

Follow the dawn carriage docket.
Go to the glass viaduct, or return to Festival Commons first.
The Dawn Carriage

The docket leads to the glass viaduct. A line of locked carriages waits above the refuge where Brass has been sheltering people.
He knows how to open the train. The warden is about to order him to leave.

WARDEN: Unload the voices.
BRASS: There are people in those carriages.
WARDEN: You signed for the cargo.
BRASS: I signed because I was afraid. I'm still afraid. Open the doors.

Brass goes from carriage to carriage until every door stands open. A boy runs past him and into his mother's arms.
Among the transport papers, Iona finds a list of river tests. The prisoners were witnesses, not criminals. Riven's signature is on the report.

BRASS: I took those papers to the well myself. Told myself it wasn't my business.
IONA: Riven's still down there.
BRASS: Then ask him. The drain stairs are below this bridge. I'll carry the papers this time—and stay to hear the answer.
Find Brass, open the prison carriages, and get their passengers to the refuge.
The train manifest connects the missing people to poisoned-water tests signed by Riven.

Follow the signed river report.
Enter the drain below the viaduct, or visit Festival Commons first.
The Undercity Well

The people on the train had complained about the water. Their test report bears Riven's name, but the clean result does not match what is flowing through the drain.
Find him at the undercity well. Before asking for an explanation, stop anyone else from drinking it.

RIVEN: The keeper's shell is caught over the filter. Every time it moves, the poison goes downstream.
SABLE: Can we get it off without wrecking the well?
RIVEN: Open the valve. I'll show you where the shell has split.

Clear water runs through the lower channels. Iona kneels to test it before anyone drinks.
Riven watches her, his hands still black with rust. When she nods, he takes out the report he signed.

RIVEN: I changed the result. They said they'd close the well and leave this quarter dry. I thought one false line would buy us time.
IONA: Who kept the real test?
RIVEN: Hesper. The chapel is up the stairs above this drain. Take me with you. She deserves to hear me say it.
Find Riven and clear the poisoned filter before more water reaches the lower city.
Riven admits falsifying the water report. Hesper kept the original account in the chapel above the drain.

Take Riven's admission to Hesper.
Climb to the chapel above the drain, or return to Festival Commons first.
Chapel of Rain

Hesper kept the water tests after Orison erased her quarter from its maps. She has been hiding in the chapel, where the ash in the bell tower reacts whenever someone speaks.
Reach her and learn how to draw it away.

The last bell rings. Ash peels from the pillars and gathers into a figure between Sable and the witness.
HESPER: That's what has been listening.
SABLE: Get her behind us. Nobody has to whisper for that thing again.

With the ash scattered, Hesper's voice carries through the roofless chapel. She names the engineer behind the collection system: Veyr.
He built an engine to reach his lost daughter. Orison made it listen to the whole city.

HESPER: Riven kept one lie alive. The archive has thousands. Mira kept the names they tried to strike out.
RIVEN: Will she believe us?
HESPER: Take her my account. The archive is east of here. And tell her I'm tired of being called a missing person.
Protect Hesper and recover the account Orison tried to erase.
Hesper identifies Veyr as the engine's designer and Mira as the keeper of the stolen names.

Bring Hesper's account to Mira.
Go east to the archive, or visit Festival Commons first.
Names in the Archive

Hesper's account names Veyr, but an accusation will not free the people still being counted as property. Mira has hidden their names inside the archive.
Reach her in the west wing, then use her key at the eastern index. We need the records intact.

MIRA: It has read their names a thousand times and never once listened to them.
SABLE: Then we stop it reading.
MIRA: Stop it destroying the pages first. Those people have already been erased once.

Mira catches the first ledger before it falls into the ink. Names, dates, and copied voices spill across the index.
The accounts do not end when a worker dies. Sable finds his mother's name among the charges. The sky engine is still collecting on her song.

MIRA: Veyr's authorization is on every transfer. He's in the sky engine's mooring office.
SABLE: The plate at Rook's bench was dated after she died. I thought—
MIRA: I know. We don't have the whole answer yet. Take the records. This time he answers to the people in them.
Recover the names and voice records without letting the archive destroy either.
The archive continues billing copied voices as labor after death. Veyr authorized their transfer to the sky engine.

Confront Veyr with the copied registrations.
Go to the sky engine, or return to Festival Commons first.
The Sky Engine

The archive records lead to Veyr's mooring office above the city. He has stopped obeying Orison, but the engine he built is still drawing voices into the spire.
Find out what it was meant to do, and how to stop it without dropping the docks onto the people below.

SKY MARSHAL: Director Veyr. Your engine is Orison property.
VEYR: Just Veyr.
SABLE: You signed for my mother's voice.
VEYR: I signed for all of them. Help me stop this, and I will stay for every question.

The marshal's command breaks. With the brake holding, Veyr releases the moorings one by one. The dock drifts clear instead of tearing free.
For the first time, refugee boats can land without passing through an Orison gate.

VEYR: I wanted to hear my daughter again. I taught the engine to hold a voice. Orison taught it to keep taking.
SABLE: So we shut it down.
VEYR: Without another source, the lower city freezes. Corin's orchard still has a living seed. If it survived the fire, we may have a way.
Make the sky dock safe and make Veyr help stop the system he designed.
Stopping extraction without cutting the city's heat requires another power source. Corin's surviving seed may provide it.

Look for Corin's living seed.
Reach the burned orchard, or visit Festival Commons first.
Orchard After Fire

The orchard was burned to expose the vein beneath its roots. Sable remembers the cordon; he was one of the people told to keep the road clear.
Corin never left. Find him, and see whether the seed Veyr remembers is still alive.

The seed rises with the scorched root wrapped around it. Its stored voices break into frightened fragments, and the burning branches lash outward.
IONA: It's defending the last thing it has.
SABLE: Then keep the water coming. We take the fire away, not the memory.

Iona lowers the seed into clean water. Its light steadies. Around them, the first green shoots push through the ash.
Sable stays beside the ruined cordon until Corin puts the water bowl into his hands.

CORIN: You can't undo the night they burned this place. You can carry something out of it alive.
SABLE: Will this keep the city warm?
VEYR: If I connect it at the reactor.
CORIN: Then go. But don't call it empty fuel. You've seen what grows here.
Help Corin cool the burned grove and recover the seed without destroying its memory.
The surviving seed offers a way to sustain the reactor without continuing to take people's voices.

Carry the living seed to the reactor.
Enter the last reactor, or return to Festival Commons first.
The Last Reactor

The seed gives us a way to stop the city's central collector without turning off its heat. Veyr knows the reactor controls; the people whose voices it holds have no way to reach them.
Isolate the chambers, cool the Crown's shield, and decide how to free what is inside.

HOLLOW CROWN: I can keep every voice. Nothing need be lost.
SABLE: You kept my mother's song. You didn't bring her home.
IONA: Let the living go.
HOLLOW CROWN: Without me, they will forget.
SABLE: Then we will remind each other.

The Crown cracks. The pull on the city's voices stops, and the seed holds the reactor's heat steady.
Sable waits for a voice he knows. Instead, he hears the people beside him calling to one another across the broken chamber.

At the docks, a message from Lowbank is waiting: children are still disappearing.
IONA: We stopped the central collector. The wards it left behind are still working.
SABLE: Then we aren't finished.
BRASS: Lowbank shelter is open. We'll start with the families who sent this.
Stop the central collector, protect the memory chambers, and keep the city warm with the living seed.
The Crown's defeat stops central extraction, but its local wards remain active. Lowbank families are still losing children.

Answer Lowbank's call for help.
Go to Lowbank shelter, or return to Festival Commons first.
The Children of Lowbank

IONA: The Crown has stopped. The water hasn't come back.
SABLE: I thought breaking it would be enough.
IONA: Lowbank thought so too. Now their children are missing. Someone heard a mother's voice calling from the old shelter.
SABLE: Then we start there. We don't get to call this over while they're still waiting.

WIREMOTHER: Outside is cold. Outside they go hungry. Here, they can stay with me.
IONA: Lark, look at me. Can you hear the rain?
WIREMOTHER: You will frighten them.
IONA: They are already frightened. Let them choose who holds their hand.

Lark waits at the shelter door until Iona offers her hand. He takes it.
LARK: Will it sound like her again?
IONA: I don't know. But you won't have to go back in alone.
For the first time since the reactor fell, Sable stops looking uphill. The people who needed him were here.

Lark turns a metal work tag over in his palm. Brass recognizes the carriage number.
BRASS: This is from the other train. The one I signed out before I left.
SABLE: Where did they take it?
BRASS: The abandoned depot. I should have told you before now.
Find Lowbank's missing children, release the shelter ward, and get them outside safely.
Lark's work tag belongs to the prison train Brass once authorized. It leads to the abandoned depot.

Follow the lead to the abandoned train depot.
Return to Festival Commons first if you need to rest.
The Last Prison Train

BRASS: I signed the departure order. I knew there were people in the carriages.
SABLE: You said you kept the refuge open.
BRASS: I did. I also sent a train away. Both are true.
SABLE: Then tell us where the keys are. We can argue with you after those doors are open.

CHAINMASTER: You wore the same seal. Do you think they'll forgive you because you changed sides?
BRASS: They don't owe me that.
CHAINMASTER: Then what are you doing here?
BRASS: Opening the train.

Brass reads the names slowly, stopping whenever someone answers. No one asks him to sit beside them. He stays on his feet.
A woman points to a name without an answer.
BRASS: I'll find out. I won't put 'unknown' beside it and call that finished.

One word appears beside the river prisoners again and again: trial. A survivor remembers the flood gates opening on a clear day.
RIVEN: Bring that list. The spillway survey will tell you what they were testing.
SABLE: You knew?
RIVEN: I knew what I was paid not to say. I'll show you where.
Take the keys from both depot patrols, open the prison carriage, and choose whether to lead the escape or save the manifest.
The train's survivors and departure records connect the river flood to a planned test. Riven can lead the crew to its survey.

Follow the lead to the old flood spillway.
Return to Festival Commons first if you need to rest.
What the River Kept

RIVEN: The water reached the lower quarter before the warning bells. I saw the order that opened the gates.
MIRA: And you called it an accident.
RIVEN: I signed the survey they gave me. The real one is still in the spillway locker.
SABLE: Then we're bringing the real one back. You can tell the families what your signature meant.

SILT CROWN: The river has covered the marks. No one will read them now.
RIVEN: I learned that excuse from people, not from you.
SILT CROWN: Stand aside.
RIVEN: I did that once.

Riven lays the survey where the families can read it. He does not point out the names of the other men who signed.
RIVEN: This one is mine.
For a while, nobody answers. He waits. The river keeps moving beside them.

The uncensored survey names Subject Seven as the keeper of the original register. Mira holds the page without folding it.
MIRA: Seven. That's what they called me.
SABLE: The name vault?
MIRA: Yes. This time we go in through the front, and we bring the names out.
Recover the uncensored flood survey, then restore the bank with Corin's cutting or reinforce the ferry landing.
The survey identifies Subject Seven—Mira—as the keeper of the original names. The next evidence is in the sealed name vault.

Follow the lead to the sealed name vault.
Return to Festival Commons first if you need to rest.
A Name Without a Number

MIRA: When they took my name, I thought someone must have kept it safe somewhere. A box. A page nobody had read.
IONA: And if it isn't there?
MIRA: I still want the others to have theirs back. I'm tired of making every locked door a promise about me.
SABLE: Then that's what we're here for. All the names we can carry.

REDACTOR: Subject Seven. You have returned to your proper place.
MIRA: My name is Mira.
REDACTOR: That name is not in the register.
MIRA: Put down your pen. I'll write it myself.

Mira finds rows of names with the same number written over them. She leaves the number on the desk.
In the empty book beside the register, she writes MIRA. There is space below it. She leaves that space alone.

Among the collector builders is Rook's father. Beside his name, someone kept the address of the house he never finished.
ROOK: I know the way.
SABLE: We can leave it until later.
ROOK: No. I've been doing that for years. Come with me.
Defeat both indexing patrols, recover the original names, and decide how to keep the register safe.
The register names Rook's father among the collector's builders and gives the address of his unfinished house.

Follow the lead to the unfinished house.
Return to Festival Commons first if you need to rest.
Rook and the Unfinished House

ROOK: He kept saying the collector would give families another chance to say goodbye. Then he stopped coming home.
SABLE: Your father?
ROOK: There's a letter upstairs. I brought it here, put it down, and found a hundred things that needed fixing first.
SABLE: We don't have to pretend this is another repair job.

HOMEKEEPER: Your father left this house for you. You should be grateful.
ROOK: He left it half-built. He left me a letter. Let me decide what those things mean.
HOMEKEEPER: I can keep it all as it was.
ROOK: That's the part I don't want.

There is no hidden instruction in the letter. His father says he was sorry. He admits what he helped build. He does not tell Rook how to forgive him.
ROOK: I wanted him to have a better reason.
SABLE: I know.
Rook folds the page along its old creases. This time, he takes it with him.

The letter describes a glass chamber made for Veyr's daughter. Rook shows him the passage.
VEYR: I told myself they were keeping her voice safe.
ROOK: I know what that story sounds like.
VEYR: Then don't let me tell it again when we get there.
Release the house circuit, sound the three studs, and reach the letter in the attic with Rook or an Ether.
Rook's father's letter identifies the glass chamber built for the recording of Veyr's daughter.

Follow the lead to the glass chamber.
Return to Festival Commons first if you need to rest.
The Daughter in the Glass

VEYR: I remember her voice more clearly than her face now. I hate admitting that.
IONA: What did the collector promise you?
VEYR: That I wouldn't lose the rest. I kept making it stronger, and called that love.
SABLE: We'll listen to what's there. Then we look outside. There is a child waiting for help.

GLASS CHILD: Papa? You said you would stay until I fell asleep.
VEYR: I did. I stayed beside your bed.
GLASS CHILD: Papa? You said—
VEYR: I know. You can't hear what I say now, can you?
IONA: Veyr. The door is behind us. We're still here.

Outside, a living girl flinches when Veyr says his daughter's name.
VEYR: I'm sorry. That wasn't fair. What should I call you?
She tells him. He repeats it once, carefully, and asks whether she is cold.
For now, that is the question he can answer.

The girl remembers the checkpoint on the mountain road. Families were separated there; the officers kept their papers.
Sable recognizes the description before she finishes.
SABLE: I carried dispatches through that gate.
MIRA: Then you can show us the road. You don't get to walk it alone either.
Recover the damaged spool, make sure the living child gets outside, and choose whether to leave with her or preserve the echo's warning.
The rescued child describes the mountain checkpoint where refugees disappeared—the same gate Sable once served as a courier.

Follow the lead to the mountain checkpoint.
Return to Festival Commons first if you need to rest.
Sable Takes Off the Uniform

SABLE: I wore their badge to get past doors. I said I only carried the messages.
MIRA: You didn't write the orders.
SABLE: No. But I learned not to ask what happened after I delivered them. The commander at this gate taught me that.
BRASS: Then let him see what you do after you stop obeying.

COMMANDER: You carried our seal. You know what desertion costs.
SABLE: I know what staying quiet costs.
COMMANDER: You'll throw away your place for these people?
SABLE: They're the ones who gave me a place. Open the gate.

Sable removes the insignia. There is no speech ready for it. He puts it in the earth beside the road.
A family waits for someone to tell them whether they can cross.
SABLE: Yes. You don't need an order.
He stays beside the gate until they believe him.

The refugees say the checkpoint's orders were answered from inside the mountain. Hesper hears the same phrase returning through the relays.
HESPER: That's why the Crown going quiet changed so little. It wasn't the only one singing.
SABLE: Show us where the answer comes from.
Defeat both checkpoint squads, then open a safe route for the refugees through the gate or sheltered supply path.
The checkpoint was receiving answers from relays within the mountain. Hesper traces the returning phrase to the resonance gallery.

Follow the lead to the resonance gallery.
Return to Festival Commons first if you need to rest.
The Mountain Learns a Song

HESPER: Listen after the checkpoint phrase. There—another relay answers it. Then another.
ROOK: How far does it go?
HESPER: Under the hills. The Crown was following a voice we haven't reached.
SABLE: Can we make it stop?
HESPER: First we have to stop answering it the way it expects.

MUTE GIANT: One voice. No quarrel. No grief.
HESPER: You heard all those people, and that was the part you wanted to keep?
MUTE GIANT: A single song cannot be divided.
HESPER: Listen properly. We aren't singing the same part.

One relay answers late. Another holds a note the first has already left. The mountain waits for them to agree. They do not.
Hesper lowers her hand.
HESPER: Good. Now it has to listen instead of finishing the line for us.

A second route appears in the answering pattern: an observatory that watches the relays.
ROOK: If it can see every line, it should show us where they meet.
SABLE: And whether it can see us coming.
HESPER: Keep that question. We're going to need it.
Learn the surveyor's phrase and sound the three resonators so the mountain can hold different voices at once.
The interrupted relay pattern reveals an observatory watching the network. Its charts may show where the Choir is listening.

Follow the lead to the buried observatory.

The Observatory Below the Sky

ROOK: The chart goes past the Crown. Sixteen branch relays, all feeding the same point above the storm.
SABLE: So everything we've broken—
ROOK: Has helped people. It just hasn't ended this. Don't give that part away.
HESPER: Repair the lens. We need a way up that doesn't deliver us exactly where it expects.

STAR READER: I have seen the path you take. This ending is the gentlest.
ROOK: For whom?
STAR READER: Fewer voices will be lost.
ROOK: You keep counting what people lose. You never ask what they choose to risk.

The repaired chart finds the Choir engine above the storm. Every forecast ends with the same command—until the lens passes over a blank crossing.
ROOK: It knows the old roads. It doesn't know every way people might use them.
SABLE: Then we need that blank.

The lens also shows lights on the eastern face: a settlement at the end of its heat supply.
IONA: They won't last until we come back down.
SABLE: Then we stop there first.
VEYR: The stormway runs beyond it. We'll need both a warm place behind us and a safe crossing ahead.
Recover the broken lens frame, repair the observatory view, and choose to chart hidden crossings or study the storm's warning.
The repaired lens locates the Choir above the storm and a freezing settlement along the approach. Reach its relief store before continuing.

Follow the lead to the mountain relief store.

The Price of Warm Rooms

DARA: The families from the lower road reached the eastern face. We found them a roof. The heat cable is nearly dead.
IONA: How many are sick?
DARA: More by morning. We can supply the clinic or get the kitchen generator running. I need you to see both needs before you choose.
SABLE: We're here. Tell us what each will take.

TOLLKEEPER: The cable belongs to the board. The board has not approved these occupants.
DARA: They walked here with children in their arms. Look at them.
TOLLKEEPER: I have a list.
DARA: Then you have something to put down.

Someone begins counting blankets. Someone else asks who can mend a roof. There is still too much to do, but tonight the room is warm.
DARA: Stay for a cup.
SABLE: Just one.
For a few minutes, nobody asks the crew to save anything else.

The settlement can keep its heat, but families are still stranded across the stormway. Its anchors were built for cargo, not passengers.
VEYR: I know the wind locks. They can be made safe.
SABLE: Then that's the next job. A road open only to us isn't an open road.
Supply the public clinic with 300 credits or power the shared kitchen with one Mid Ether.
The settlement now has a warm room. To connect it to the remaining refugees, the crew must secure the stormway anchors.

A Sky Full of Borrowed Wings

VEYR: Those hooks carried ore. Nobody cared whether the load arrived frightened.
BRASS: A carriage isn't so different.
VEYR: It ought to be. People need somewhere to put their feet and time to let go.
SABLE: Show us the locks. We won't send anyone across a route we haven't opened ourselves.

WIND BAILIFF: Passenger loads are forbidden.
VEYR: Then we'll change what the crossing is for.
WIND BAILIFF: You do not own the stormway.
VEYR: Neither do the people you left on the other side. That's why we're opening it.

Cargo hooks hold the first handrail. The pilot tests it twice before calling the families forward.
Veyr waits beside the last crossing. When someone asks whether it is safe, he gives an honest answer and stays to help them through.

Across the stormway, a message from the northern court repeats a witness's voice. The words have been cut apart.
MIRA: That's not a hearing. They've already written the verdict.
SABLE: Can we reach the witnesses?
MIRA: The vault below the court. Before they make those voices say anything else.
Learn the pilot's wind-lock phrase and secure the storm anchorage so people can use the cargo crossing safely.
The secured stormway reaches the northern court, where the board is cutting stolen testimony into a false verdict. Find the witness vault.

The Trial of the Witnesses

MIRA: They kept the witnesses in a vault and brought only their voices to court. If a sentence was inconvenient, they cut it.
SABLE: We have the train evidence. The flood survey. The names.
MIRA: Yes. And some of it will make people hate us too. We don't get to make the same cuts because we're frightened of what they'll hear.

FALSE JUDGE: These accounts contradict each other. They cannot all be true.
MIRA: They remember different parts. Let them finish.
FALSE JUDGE: The court requires agreement.
MIRA: Then the court can learn to wait.

The accounts go out with their pauses, their anger, and their disagreements intact. Some witnesses sign. Others need their names protected.
Nobody offers Mira a tidy ending. For the first time, she does not try to find one in the pages.

The witnesses describe the first pottery floor, where the collector learned to smooth every difference out of a voice.
ROOK: My father worked from that mold. If the old marks survived, I can read what the later copies lost.
SABLE: Then we go back to the beginning of the machine—not the beginning of us.
Defeat both vault wardens, release the unedited testimony, and decide whether the witnesses' names should be public or protected.
The freed testimony identifies the first pottery floor and the mold used to erase differences between recorded voices.

The Clay That Refused the Mold

ROOK: Before there were collectors in every district, there was this. Clay under someone's fingers.
SABLE: Can it tell us who recorded my mother after she died?
ROOK: It can tell us when one recording became many. I won't promise you more than that.
SABLE: Good. I need you to tell me what's here, not what I want to hear.

FIRST FORM: The marks are faults. I can remove them. I can make the voice whole.
IONA: You can make the copies match. That isn't the same thing.
FIRST FORM: Difference causes pain.
IONA: So does holding someone still when they are trying to leave.

The first mold keeps its rough edges. Separate sessions appear where the later copies had been pressed into one smooth surface.
Rook reads the dates without softening them. Sable listens.
There is no hidden life waiting in the clay. There is a record of what was taken.

A mark beneath the mold identifies the intake that feeds the Choir. Brass follows its line to the mines.
BRASS: Workers are still down there. The engine is taking their air.
SABLE: Then we open it outward. The machine can wait for us this time.
Follow the potter's five-note phrase and preserve the first mold's old marks instead of smoothing them away.

Where the Choir Takes Breath

BRASS: That is a work lamp. There's another below it. The mines aren't empty.
IONA: The intake is drawing their air uphill.
BRASS: I know the pump. If I can turn it, they'll have a way to breathe while they climb out.
SABLE: We don't touch the Choir until those people can reach the sky.

CHOIR LUNG: The city must remember. The intake must remain open.
BRASS: Those are people below you.
CHOIR LUNG: The city must remember.
BRASS: I heard the order. I'm not obeying it.

The first worker reaches daylight with an unlit lamp. Brass takes it so she can use both hands to climb.
More lamps follow. He does not count the ones still below as losses. He goes back to the edge and waits for the next hand.

The workers point out the common assembly above the vent house. People have gathered there to decide who will keep the records when the Choir is gone.
DARA: They need an answer before you go into that chamber. Otherwise someone will call the empty chair theirs.
SABLE: Then we meet them first.
Restore the mine air pump with Brass or an Ether, then finish the vent phrase and turn the intake outward.
The freed workers lead the crew to the common assembly, where the city must decide how to keep its records after the Choir.

The City Chooses Its Voices

DARA: They've been arguing all morning. It is the best sound I've heard up here.
SABLE: About who takes the Choir's place?
DARA: About how we stop anyone taking it. An archive people can enter. A school where the songs keep changing. We can begin one now.
MIRA: Then let the people who have to live with it be heard.

CHOIR HAND: Without a keeper, the records will be lost.
DARA: Without a door, they were already lost to the people in them.
CHOIR HAND: Who will answer for them?
DARA: We will. More than one of us. That's the part you never allowed.

The first instructions leaving the assembly are practical: bring shelves, find teachers, tell the families when the room will open.
Then other voices answer with things the plan forgot. Nobody shuts them off.
Sable listens until he hears that the work will continue without him.

Word travels down the mountain before the Choir can call it an order. A public beginning now exists outside the machine.
HESPER: The listening chamber is ahead. When you answer, leave a gap at the end.
SABLE: For the city?
HESPER: For whoever hasn't spoken yet.
Help establish the common archive with 300 credits or the river school with one Mid Ether, then release the route to the listening chamber.
The common assembly begins a public alternative to the Choir. With that work underway, the crew can enter the listening chamber without leaving an empty throne behind.

Follow the lead to the listening chamber.

A Song With No Last Note

Above the storm, the Choir carries every voice it has taken. Sable can hear his mother's phrase among them. It sounds no closer than it did at the first clay reader.
IONA: You don't have to pretend you don't want to hear her.
SABLE: I want to hear her. I don't want that wanting to decide what happens to everyone else.
HESPER: Then answer with the voices that came here with you.

THE CHOIR: If I stop, they will forget. The names. The dead. Each other.
SABLE: We will forget things. We'll get them wrong.
THE CHOIR: I can keep them perfect.
SABLE: You kept them from us. Open your hands.
IONA: We'll help one another remember.

The Choir leaves a space where its last order should have been. One person answers, then another, neither repeating the first exactly.
Below the mountain, the city takes up the phrase. Sable waits for his mother's voice to tell him what to do.
It does not. At last, he is ready to choose without it.

The city's records remain, but no single machine can make every voice begin again. The archive work, the school, the warm rooms, and the roads will need living hands.
Sable has one smaller promise left.
SABLE: Mara's waiting for the reed case. I'm going home.
Learn Hesper's answering phrase, prepare the crew on the approach, and confront the Choir together.
The Choir can no longer dictate the city's answer. The crew returns the future to living people; Sable must decide what to do with the recording his mother freely left.
